stem: A client with a spinal cord injury is beginning rehabilitation. Which nursing approach best supports mobility and functional independence?

options.A: Coordinate an individualized rehabilitation plan based on the client's impairments and goals, reinforce prescribed mobility and range-of-motion activities, and address assistive-equipment needs with the rehabilitation team.
options.B: Use a standard transfer and mobility plan for clients with similar spinal cord injuries, then adjust it only if the client cannot complete the expected exercises or activities of daily living.
options.C: Postpone range-of-motion work and trials of assistive equipment until neurologic recovery has stabilized, while focusing early nursing care mainly on preventing medical complications.
options.D: Leave transfer training, positioning, and mobility practice to rehabilitation therapists and limit nursing participation to reinforcing safety instructions after therapy sessions are completed.

rationale: Current NICE rehabilitation guidance states that rehabilitation programmes should be tailored to the person's individual needs and short- and long-term goals and should include appropriate physical and occupational therapies. NICE also recommends promoting independence in activities of daily living, maintaining joint range of motion after spinal cord injury, considering progressive sitting and specialized equipment to increase mobility, and assessing assistive-technology needs without delay. Therefore A is correct because it integrates individualized goals with ongoing nursing reinforcement and multidisciplinary rehabilitation. B incorrectly substitutes a standardized plan for individualized rehabilitation. C delays range-of-motion and assistive-technology interventions that NICE recommends addressing during rehabilitation rather than waiting for neurologic recovery to stabilize. D creates an artificial separation between therapy and nursing care; the NCLEX blueprint explicitly includes nursing assistance with activities of daily living, positioning, assistive devices, range of motion, and mobilization.
educational_objective: Support spinal cord injury rehabilitation with an individualized, goal-directed plan that reinforces prescribed mobility and range-of-motion activities, promotes independence in daily activities, and coordinates assistive-equipment needs with the rehabilitation team.
source_organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source_version_date: Published January 18, 2022; current NICE guidance accessed 2026-08-25
source_locator: Recommendations 1.5.1: rehabilitation programmes should be tailored to individual needs and goals and include appropriate physical and occupational therapies. 1.11.9: promote independence with activities of daily living. Section 1.15 Rehabilitation after spinal cord injury > Maintaining mobility and movement: 1.15.23 maintain joint range of motion; 1.15.25 consider progressive sitting or tilt-table interventions to increase mobility and aid early sitting; 1.15.26 consider specialized equipment to promote mobility, upper-limb function and independent walking; 1.15.27 assess needs and refer without delay when assistive technology is required.
source_claim_supported: Spinal cord injury rehabilitation should be individualized and goal directed, should preserve joint range of motion and promote mobility and daily-function independence, and should address specialized equipment and assistive-technology needs without unnecessary delay.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort, printed p. 35: assess client performance of activities of daily living and assist when needed; assist client to compensate for a physical or sensory impairment using assistive devices or positioning; implement measures to promote circulation such as active or passive range of motion, positioning and mobilization. Related Assistive Devices content includes assessing and managing the client's use of assistive devices and evaluating correct use.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — mobility, activities of daily living, range of motion, positioning, and assistive-device support during spinal cord injury rehabilitation
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four approaches to remove the keyed-answer length cue and the distractor-only absolute wording. The revised distractors are realistic rehabilitation errors involving standardized goals, delayed mobility/assistive interventions, and inappropriate separation of nursing from mobility and functional care.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Spinal cord injury rehabilitation — mobility and functional independence
audit_findings.stem: PASS — asks for the nursing approach that best supports mobility and function during rehabilitation without assuming a fixed neurologic level or universal equipment prescription.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects individualized goal-based rehabilitation, maintenance of range of motion, mobility progression, and coordinated assistive-technology planning; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — standardized pathways may aid organization, but NICE requires rehabilitation to be tailored to the individual's needs and goals rather than using a default functional target until failure occurs.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — medical-complication prevention remains important, but delaying range-of-motion and assistive-technology planning conflicts with NICE recommendations to maintain motion and assess technology needs during rehabilitation without unnecessary delay.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — specialist therapists are central to rehabilitation, but nursing also participates in ADL assistance, positioning, assistive-device support, range of motion, mobilization, and reinforcement of the rehabilitation plan.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that combines individualized goals, current mobility/ROM support, and multidisciplinary assistive-equipment planning without adding delay or role fragmentation.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B defaults to standardized goals, C delays recommended rehabilitation elements, and D inappropriately removes nursing from ongoing functional care.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — alternatives are comparable in length and clinical detail; no distractor-only absolute term or obviously absurd mechanism remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes ADL assistance, assistive devices, positioning, range of motion, and mobilization.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether early rehabilitation should wait for neurologic stability or be delegated primarily to therapy. NICE specifically supports individualized rehabilitation, ongoing joint-range preservation, mobility progression, and prompt assistive-technology assessment, while NCSBN explicitly includes nursing mobility and ADL functions; A remains uniquely best.
